plot_extraction.response_text:
During a plague outbreak in medieval London, two drunken sailors, the tall, gaunt Legs and the short, stout Hugh Tarpaulin, flee an alehouse without paying. Pursued by the landlady, they climb a barricade into a quarantined, disease-ridden district and wander through its abandoned streets.

They enter an undertaker’s shop, where six grotesquely costumed drunkards are feasting among coffins, skulls, and a suspended skeleton. Their leader calls himself King Pest and presents the others as his royal family, claiming they are conducting solemn research into the city’s alcoholic treasures in service of Death. He punishes the sailors’ intrusion by ordering each to drink a gallon of strong liquor or be drowned in a barrel of ale.

Legs refuses, while Tarpaulin exposes the supposed king as a stage actor named Tim Hurlygurly. The enraged group cries treason, and the “queen” throws Tarpaulin into the ale barrel. Legs retaliates by knocking the king into the cellar, attacking the company with the hanging skeleton, and overturning the barrel to rescue his companion. The resulting flood wrecks the room, kills or sweeps away several members of the mock court, and throws the rest into chaos. Legs and Tarpaulin then escape toward their ship, each carrying off one of the women.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts a mock-Gothic, grotesquely comic style, combining plague-era horror with farce, nautical humour, and satire of aristocratic ceremony. Its atmosphere is ostensibly macabre—abandoned streets, decaying buildings, corpses, pestilential vapours, coffins, skeletons, and personifications of disease—but the horror is repeatedly undercut by drunken bravado, slapstick violence, verbal absurdity, and extravagant caricature. The prevailing tone is therefore one of comic dread: death remains materially present, yet its symbols are converted into costumes, drinking vessels, furniture, and props.

The narrative voice is conspicuously intrusive, urbane, and ironic. The narrator pauses to evaluate characters, qualify claims, and address the act of storytelling through phrases such as “I think,” “to say the truth,” and “This company I will endeavor to delineate one by one.” This creates the manner of a formal chronicler recounting ridiculous events with exaggerated seriousness. Elevated historical narration is deliberately applied to drunken escapades, while seamen are called “our friends,” “our heroes,” and “the worthy couple,” producing a sustained mock-heroic effect. Understatement and ceremonious phrasing make crude actions seem grand, and narrative dignity repeatedly clashes with physical chaos.

The diction is ornate, archaic, and Latinate. Words such as “peregrinations,” “cachinnatory,” “physiognomy,” “habiliments,” “mulct,” and “paraphernalia” lend the prose an antiquarian and pseudo-scholarly texture. Courtly formulas—“Serene Consort,” “undivided empire,” “sacred and lofty purposes”—are juxtaposed with tavern language, insults, curses, and sailor slang. The seamen speak in an extended nautical idiom, describing drinking and bodily capacity through “cargo,” “ballast,” “hold,” “stowage-room,” “bilge-water,” and similar shipboard metaphors. This contrast between royal bombast and maritime vernacular is one of the story’s principal comic engines.

The syntax is elaborate and highly periodic. Sentences often accumulate subordinate clauses, parenthetical qualifications, parallel phrases, and delayed conclusions. Dashes are used heavily to interrupt, amplify, or redirect the prose, creating a voice that seems both ceremonious and excitable. Descriptive passages proceed through catalogues and escalating sequences, while repeated constructions—“onward—still onward,” “more noisome and more horrible,” or the chorus of “Treason!”—build rhythm and theatrical intensity. Exclamation marks, emphatic italics or quotation marks, direct interjections, and deliberately overextended speeches give the writing an oratorical, performative quality.

Characterisation is dominated by visual caricature and oppositional design. Legs is impossibly tall, thin, solemn, and angular; Hugh Tarpaulin is short, round, purple, mobile, and irrepressibly amused. The plague court is constructed on the same principle of bodily exaggeration. Each figure is associated with a single grotesquely enlarged feature or pathological condition: forehead, mouth, nose, ears, dropsy, consumption, gout, paralysis, or delirium. Bodies are compared to barrels, bladders, ship fittings, mountains, fish, and turtles. These similes are vivid but intentionally undignified, reducing supposedly exalted personages to distorted flesh and comic machinery.

The imagery is tactile, theatrical, and morbidly decorative. The plague district is rendered through mist, rank grass, broken paving stones, collapsing beams, poisonous smells, skeletons, and rotting bodies. Inside the undertaker’s shop, death becomes a stage set: skulls serve as cups, coffin-trestles as chairs, a thigh-bone as a sceptre, a pall as a cloak, a coffin as clothing, and a suspended skeleton as a lamp. Light is typically “ghastly,” “fitful,” or vapourous, heightening the Gothic chiaroscuro. Yet these details are so excessive and inventively arranged that they create spectacle rather than pure terror.

The story’s structure moves from realistic tavern comedy into forbidden urban horror, then into a carnivalesque court scene, and finally into explosive slapstick. The early passages establish the protagonists through physical description and drunken misadventure. A substantial historical digression enlarges the plague setting and generates suspense. The centre of the story slows into a tableau, introducing the six members of the Pest family one by one. Dialogue then turns the tableau into a mock trial or royal council, after which recognition of the “king” as an actor punctures the supernatural pretence. The conclusion accelerates sharply into brawling, flooding, drowning, overturned furniture, and comic escape.

Dialogue is strongly differentiated by social register. King Pest speaks in pompous, balanced proclamations filled with abstractions and royal plurals, whereas Legs and Tarpaulin answer with blunt irreverence and maritime slang. The Pest family often speaks chorally, making them resemble actors in a grotesque stage performance. Names such as “Pest-Iferous,” “Pest-Ilential,” “Tem-Pest,” and “Ana-Pest” rely on conspicuous punning, reinforcing the artificiality of the court. The revelation that its monarch is a stage-player confirms that authority here is costume, rhetoric, and performance rather than genuine sovereignty.

The humour depends on incongruity, repetition, hyperbole, and bathos. Terrifying circumstances fail to frighten the protagonists because they are too drunk to understand them; solemn speeches are interrupted by practical concerns about alcohol; royal punishments become drinking challenges; and a supposedly infernal monarch is exposed as a theatrical impostor. Violence is treated with cartoonish speed and detachment. Even drowning and brain-smashing are absorbed into the hectic comic finale rather than allowed tragic weight.

Thematically, the prose mocks pretension, hierarchy, superstition, and the ceremonial denial of bodily mortality. Disease and death form a counterfeit royal family, but sailors who treat death through familiar maritime idiom prove less vulnerable to its mystique. Aristocratic insignia are repurposed as clothing, sacred ritual becomes intoxication, and plague terror shelters theft and revelry. The style’s defining signature is this continual collision of the elevated with the debased: ornate narration describes vulgar action, Gothic horror becomes carnival, and regal authority collapses beneath laughter, drink, and physical disorder.

## The Court Beyond the Barricade

It was in the autumn of that memorable year when the bells of London had grown hoarse with tolling, and when every respectable citizen who possessed either a horse, a country cousin, or a sound pair of heels had prudently removed his person from the metropolis, that two mariners belonging to the *Saucy Wench*, a merchant brig then lying below the bridge, found themselves at midnight in the tap-room of the Crooked Bishop.

The taller of the pair—who, from the prodigious extension of his lower members, had acquired among his companions the concise and appropriate appellation of Legs—was an object which no reasonable observer could have contemplated without some astonishment. He stood six feet seven inches in his stockings; yet Nature, having expended herself upon his altitude, had neglected almost every other dimension. His knees were knots upon ropes; his elbows appeared contrivances for hanging garments; his shoulders projected like the broken yards of a dismantled vessel; and his head, which was narrow, lantern-jawed, and furnished with a melancholy quantity of reddish hair, nodded perpetually at the summit of his person, as a signal-lamp nods in a gale.

Hugh Tarpaulin, on the contrary, had been built upon principles of economy in height and prodigality in circumference. He was four feet nine, perhaps four feet ten when indignation elevated him; but across the beam he possessed the dimensions of a small beer-cask. His cheeks, naturally round, had been improved by liquor into globes of a rich Tyrian purple; his eyes rolled in their sockets with the lively independence of two peas upon a trencher; and his mouth, which extended nearly from ear to ear, seemed expressly constructed for drinking, singing, laughing, swearing, and the consumption of salt beef in unequal proportions. If Legs resembled a mast, Hugh resembled its buoy; if one was a compass-needle, the other was the compass-box; and if either had fallen overboard, the first must inevitably have gone down by the head, while the second could hardly have been persuaded to sink at all.

These worthy persons had, during the earlier part of the evening, applied themselves to the serious extermination of several measures of ale, three black-jacks of spiced wine, a flask which the hostess affirmed to be Spanish, and a smaller bottle which no one affirmed to be anything. Having reached that agreeable elevation of spirit at which a man considers his purse an impertinence and his creditor a personal enemy, they called for a final quart, drank it with a gravity becoming the ceremony, and proceeded toward the door.

“Hold!” cried Mistress Gudgeon, proprietress of the Crooked Bishop, placing before the exit a person as broad, if not quite so spherical, as Tarpaulin’s own. “Hold, you bilge-fed sons of a rotten galley! Who pays?”

Legs gazed down upon her from his eminence.

“Madam,” said he, with a mournful dignity, “the question is improperly timed.”

“Improperly timed?”

“Entirely. Payment is a morning operation. We are now engaged in midnight.”

“You are engaged in robbery!” screamed Mistress Gudgeon.

Hugh put his thumb to his nose and expanded his fingers in the manner of a fan.

“Put it in the ship’s account,” said he. “Charge it to wind, weather, and His Majesty’s fishes.”

“I’ll charge it to your hides!”

She snatched up a pewter measure and launched it with such precision that it passed through the interval between Legs’s knees and inflicted a considerable insult upon a gentleman sleeping beneath the table. The gentleman arose with a howl. The hostess shouted “Thieves!” Legs overturned a bench. Hugh seized a cold pudding for ballast. Two drawers, a fiddler, the insulted sleeper, and a dog with no apparent interest in finance joined the pursuit; and our heroes, issuing into the night with that suddenness peculiar to men who discover that an account has been kept, ran eastward through a confusion of lanes.

Now, to say the truth, neither sailor could have explained why he ran eastward rather than westward, northward, upward, or directly into the Thames. Legs maintained afterward that he steered by a certain star; but the star in question was a swinging lantern, and his course described so many triangles that no geometer would have admitted it as navigation. Hugh followed because Hugh’s legs, once excited, were incapable of immediate deliberation.

Behind them came Mistress Gudgeon, crying murder; behind Mistress Gudgeon came the drawers; behind the drawers came the fiddler; and behind all came the dog, who had now decided that the whole business was political.

Onward went the mariners—down Fishbone Alley, across Saint Mortimer’s Close, through a court in which seven cats held parliament, and into a street so narrow that Legs, swaying from side to side, polished both walls with his shoulders. At the farther end rose a barricade of timber, paving stones, broken carts, and household furniture, crowned at intervals by spikes. Upon it hung a board bearing, in letters legible even to sobriety:

**PESTILENCE WITHIN.  
BY ORDER OF THE LORD MAYOR,  
NO MAN SHALL ENTER OR DEPART  
ON PAIN OF DEATH.**

A red cross, newly painted, sprawled beneath the proclamation.

Hugh stopped.

“Legs,” said he, “there’s a lee shore.”

“There’s an elevation,” replied Legs, contemplating the obstacle with one eye. “We ascend.”

“Did you read the cargo manifest?”

“I never read when pursued. It confuses the judgment.”

Mistress Gudgeon appeared at the mouth of the street, brandishing a ladle. Her reinforcement clattered behind her.

The barricade, viewed under these circumstances, lost much of its objectionable character. Legs mounted it in three long motions, resembling a spider climbing a cupboard. Tarpaulin scrambled after him, assisted from below by the point of the landlady’s ladle and from above by a grip upon his collar. The timbers groaned; a chair collapsed; Hugh rolled over the summit; Legs toppled after; and both descended upon the forbidden side amid a cataract of stones, crockery, and one wooden image of Saint Giles.

Their pursuers came no farther. Mistress Gudgeon, though courageous in matters of credit, entertained orthodox opinions respecting contagion. She stood beyond the barrier, poured forth a final broadside of maledictions, and retired with her fleet, leaving the dog to bark twice at the proclamation and then follow more sensible company.

The sailors rose.

Before them lay a district upon which silence had settled, not as snow settles, lightly and with purity, but as a damp cloth is thrown over the face of a corpse. No lamp burned in any casement. The moon, half strangled in a yellow vapour, revealed rows of leaning houses whose upper stories approached one another like conspirators. Doors hung open; shutters beat intermittently against walls; weeds pierced the paving; and from the gutters arose an odour compounded of wet straw, extinguished fires, spoiled victuals, old medicines, and that final corruption which even drunkenness recognizes, though it may decline to name it.

This part of London had been closed for fourteen days.

The sickness, which began modestly in a cellar and afterward displayed all the ambition of a conqueror, had passed from house to house with such celerity that men who breakfasted in tolerable health were measured for winding-sheets before supper. Physicians disputed concerning vapours, conjunctions, divine displeasure, subterranean exhalations, and the excessive consumption of onions; but the plague, unmoved by argument, continued its rounds. Nurses fled from patients, priests from parishes, heirs from benefactors. Whole families disappeared behind doors marked with the red cross. Carts went groaning through the streets at dawn, collecting their melancholy freight. When drivers themselves fell dead, the horses wandered unattended until they overturned among the pits.

At length the authorities, finding every measure ineffectual except the measure which placed danger at a convenient distance, enclosed the most afflicted quarter with barricades. The healthy were kept out, the sick were kept in, and civic wisdom congratulated itself upon having separated misery from observation.

Into this region, then, Legs and Hugh Tarpaulin had entered; and I think it no injustice to their understanding to state that several minutes passed before they perceived any alteration in the general character of the night.

Hugh recovered the pudding, which had survived the descent in a flattened condition, and tucked it beneath his arm.

“Quiet anchorage,” he observed.

“Too quiet,” replied Legs.

“Every berth shut.”

“Maybe the watch is asleep.”

“Then we’ll not wake him.”

They proceeded.

At the first crossing they encountered an abandoned handcart containing three covered shapes. Tarpaulin lifted a corner of the cloth, looked beneath it, replaced it, and touched his cap.

“Passengers,” said he. “All bound one way.”

Farther on, a corpse sat upright against a pump, as though waiting for someone to bring a cup. A bundle lay in a doorway and began to cough; but when Legs bent over it, the coughing ceased. From an upper window came a low laugh—whether human, mechanical, or merely the wind contending with a hinge, our heroes did not determine. They increased their pace, though each afterward denied having done so.

The vapour thickened. It crawled around their ankles, entered cellars, issued from drains, and collected in the hollows of the street. Once Hugh stepped upon something soft and round. It burst with a melancholy sigh. He swore that it was a bladder; Legs, who had seen the tuft of hair attached to it, preserved a charitable silence.

“Legs,” said Hugh presently, “this cruise lacks society.”

“Our late society was too attentive.”

“A man wants moderation. I dislike a street where everybody asks for money, but I dislike one where nobody asks for anything. It has an uncommercial air.”

They turned into Bell-and-Bone Lane, where the houses had suffered grievously from neglect. Beams projected like broken ribs; roofs sagged; plaster had fallen away in leprous patches. A sign representing an angel with a shovel swung overhead, and beneath it stood an undertaker’s establishment. The windows were boarded; the door appeared shut; yet from within came a glow, a murmur of voices, and—most persuasive of all to the nautical intellect—the clinking of vessels.

Hugh raised a finger.

“Cargo shifting.”

“Glass cargo,” said Legs.

“Liquid cargo.”

“Contraband, perhaps.”

“Then it needs honest inspection.”

They approached. The door, when pushed, yielded with a long complaint; and our friends entered a narrow passage lined on either side by coffins standing upright. Some were plain, some richly nailed, some no larger than fiddle cases. A black cloth brushed Hugh’s face. Legs struck his forehead against the crossed bones of a funeral hatchment and brought down a shower of dust, two wooden cherubs, and a dead rat of venerable appearance.

At the passage end was a second door, from behind which issued a voice of great magnificence:

“—and therefore, beloved sister, the purple vintage of the southern province must be reserved for our anatomical experiments, while the brown ale of the northern ward may properly be surrendered to the household.”

“Hear!” cried several voices.

“Anatomy,” whispered Hugh. “That’s drinking with long words.”

He opened the door.

The apartment beyond had once served for the display and preparation of funerary merchandise, but it had lately been arranged with an originality which merits particular description. In the centre stood a long table composed of coffin lids laid across trestles. Upon it smoked an enormous bowl of punch, flanked by bottles, stone jars, flagons, onions, candles, dice, cold meats, and two human skulls employed as drinking cups. Coffins, placed horizontally, served as seats; others, turned upright, formed cupboards. A funeral pall had been stretched against one wall as a tapestry, while wreaths, hatchments, shrouds, and little leaden plates bearing the names of deceased persons constituted the remaining decorations.

From a beam depended a complete skeleton. A candle had been fixed within its skull, and the flame, shining through the eye-holes and chattering teeth, bestowed upon the entire room that fitful and ghastly illumination which persons of taste prefer at an entertainment devoted to mortality.

Around the table sat six individuals.

This company I will endeavour to delineate one by one; for it is in the accurate inventory of wonders that the conscientious historian differs from the ordinary liar.

At the head sat a man whose stature, though inferior to that of Legs, was rendered imposing by the prodigious elevation of his forehead. This forehead rose above his eyebrows in successive polished terraces, until it vanished beneath a crown manufactured from a brass warming-pan. His face below was narrow and blue; his eyes were sunk deeply; and his mouth, being both thin and habitually pursed, suggested that he had spent his life whistling at funerals. He wore a black velvet actor’s doublet, a scarlet petticoat over one shoulder by way of mantle, and about his neck a chain composed of coffin handles. In his right hand he carried a sceptre fashioned from a thigh-bone, at the top of which had been attached a pewter knob.

At his side reclined a lady of uncommon amplitude. Her body, inflated by either dropsy, beer, upholstery, or a coalition of the three, spread across two coffins and threatened a third. She wore a widow’s veil, a stomacher embroidered with silver skulls, and a necklace of small apothecaries’ bottles. Her cheeks were dead white; her lips were vermilion; and her single visible eye regarded the world with the moist severity of an oyster. Upon her head sat a coronet of horses’ teeth. This was the queen.

Opposite her was a gentleman composed chiefly of nose. That organ descended, purple and mountainous, over his mouth, forcing his words to emerge from either side in separate currents. He was clad from chin to heel in a child’s coffin, through which holes had been cut for his head, arms, and legs; and he sat so stiffly that whenever he desired drink he was obliged to topple forward until his nose entered the bowl. His title, as we later learned, was His Grace the Archduke Pest-Ulent.

Beside the archduke perched a thin young woman with a neck like a heron and ears of such dimensions that they seemed less parts of her head than handles by which the head might be carried away. Her gown was made of stitched winding-sheets. A string of little bells encircled her waist, tinkling at every breath; and a pair of spectacles without glass rested on the point of her chin. She was Princess Ana-Pest, patroness of fevers, fainting-fits, and devotional music.

The fifth personage was a small old man, yellow, wrinkled, and bent nearly double by gout. His feet were wrapped in funeral cushions, his hands trembled, and his lower jaw moved without interruption, though no sound proceeded from it except at irregular intervals, when he barked like a fox. A mitre constructed from folded death notices adorned his head. This ecclesiastic was the Grand Pestifer, spiritual adviser to the crown.

The sixth and last was a youth—or perhaps a very old woman; the matter remains in controversy—whose face was red on one side and green on the other. One eye stared upward, the second inward. His or her limbs performed small independent dances beneath a coat of hearse-plumes, and from the shoulders projected two black boards inscribed “AGED 19” and “DIED SUDDENLY.” This creature was Tem-Pest, royal infant and presumptive heir.

When Legs and Tarpaulin entered, the six turned toward them with one motion, save Tem-Pest, whose head turned first, whose eyes followed separately, and whose body completed the manoeuvre after an interval.

There ensued a silence.

Hugh removed the crushed pudding from beneath his arm, placed it politely upon the table, and looked into the punch bowl.

“Evening,” said he.

The man in the warming-pan crown rose. His height increased by reason of the forehead until the crown scraped the skeleton’s toes.

“Profane and inexplicable intruders!” he began. “By what negligence of our sentinels, what audacity of your own degraded natures, or what especial interposition of the universal monarch whom we serve, have you penetrated the sacred privacy of our court?”

Legs glanced over his shoulder at the empty passage.

“Sentinels asleep,” he said.

“Treason!” cried the queen.

“Treason!” squeaked Ana-Pest.

“Treason!” barked the Grand Pestifer.

“Treason!” shouted the archduke, one half of the word issuing from each side of his nose.

Tem-Pest clapped and fell beneath the table.

“Peace!” commanded the crowned man, striking the thigh-bone upon a skull. “We are King Pest the First—sovereign of vapours, prince of pustules, lord of the lazar-house, hereditary duke of decomposition, and by the especial favour of Death, emperor of this abandoned ward. The majestic lady at our right is our serene consort, Queen Pest-Iferous. The remainder, as their physiognomies should have informed even minds pickled in salt water, constitute our august family.”

Tarpaulin bowed to the punch.

“Very august,” said he. “Especially the old bottle with the nose.”

The archduke attempted to rise. His coffin caught against the table, and he fell backward with his feet in the air.

“Treason!” cried the family once more.

Legs placed one long hand upon Hugh’s shoulder.

“Mind your tongue,” he said. “We are in foreign waters.”

“We are in an undertaker’s back room.”

“Same thing, often.”

King Pest resumed his seat, arranging his petticoat-mantle with dignity.

“Since it is evident,” said he, “that ignorance rather than diplomacy has brought you before our throne, we shall require your names, conditions, nationalities, purposes, opinions respecting mortality, and the precise cubic capacity of your stomachs.”

“Legs,” said Legs.

“Hugh Tarpaulin,” said Hugh. “Able-bodied seaman, except in the morning.”

“Your purpose?”

“Seeking the ship.”

“Your opinions respecting mortality?”

“Bad for business.”

“And the cubic capacity of your stomach?”

Hugh considered.

“That depends on the liquor. Ale rides light. Wine goes lower. Brandy can be stowed in odd corners. Water I never take aboard unless the hold is afire.”

The royal family nodded gravely, as though this answer displayed considerable science.

King Pest then turned toward Legs.

“And you?”

“My hold,” replied the tall sailor, “is deep but narrow. I take cargo by the glass, not the flood.”

The queen whispered in her husband’s ear, though, owing to the amplitude of her person, the operation resembled a feather-bed rolling against a poker. The king listened; the Grand Pestifer barked; Ana-Pest jingled; the archduke recovered his vertical position; and Tem-Pest crawled from beneath the table with a marrow-bone in its mouth.

“Mariners,” said King Pest at length, “your arrival, though irregular, may not be wholly unpropitious. Know that this court is assembled for purposes at once philosophical, medicinal, sacramental, and fiscal. When the timid inhabitants deserted these streets, they abandoned cellars whose contents, if neglected, would inevitably fall into decay. We, who despise vulgar fear, have dedicated ourselves to a solemn examination of those alcoholic treasures. Each cask is tasted, classified, debated, and, where necessary, consumed, in honour of Death, our overlord.”

“Public service,” murmured Hugh.

“Of the loftiest description. We have investigated seven taverns, four monasteries, two private collections, the buttery of a bishop, and the medicine chest of a deceased surgeon. The sacrifices have been severe. His Grace the archduke lost consciousness in a barrel of malmsey. Our royal infant has not spoken intelligibly since Tuesday. Her Majesty has expanded three inches in the service of science.”

The queen laid a hand upon her bosom and shed a tear into a skull.

“Nevertheless,” continued the king, “our work proceeds. Authority, however, must be maintained. You have burst without announcement into the imperial presence; you have failed to kneel; you have introduced a pudding of republican appearance; and you have referred to our blood relation as an old bottle.”

“The nose misled me,” said Hugh.

“Silence! For these offences the law prescribes death.”

“Harsh anchorage,” observed Legs.

“Yet our clemency is commensurate with our power. Each offender shall be permitted a choice. Before the great clock in Saint Gaspard’s tower strikes one, he shall drink, without rest or spillage, one gallon of our green usquebaugh. If he accomplish the feat, he shall be pardoned, ennobled, and appointed Inspector of Cellars. If he fails, he shall be immersed head downward in that barrel of brown ale until the obstinacy departs from his body.”

The king pointed his sceptre toward an immense cask standing near the wall. Its top had been removed. The liquid within, black beneath the candlelight, trembled gently whenever the bells on Ana-Pest’s gown stirred.

Hugh’s eyes brightened.

“One gallon each?”

“One.”

“Is there more?”

The queen uttered a cachinnatory squeal. The archduke thumped his coffin. Even the Grand Pestifer ceased chewing his own jaw long enough to grin.

Legs, however, regarded the green liquor, which had been brought forward in two funeral jars, with profound dissatisfaction. It smoked faintly and had already begun to remove the varnish from the table.

“No,” said he.

The court became still.

King Pest leaned forward. “No?”

“No gallon.”

“Do you reject our mercy?”

“I reject the cargo. That stuff would eat the copper off a ship’s bottom.”

“It is the royal usquebaugh.”

“It is bilge-water with ambition.”

The queen gasped so violently that one of her apothecary bottles entered her mouth. Ana-Pest beat her ears with both hands. The archduke’s nose deepened from purple to black.

Hugh, meanwhile, had been studying the king. He moved to the left. The king turned away. Hugh moved to the right. The king drew his mantle over his face. Tarpaulin placed both fists upon his hips.

“Sink me,” he said slowly, “if I don’t know that forehead.”

King Pest struck the table.

“Guards!”

No guards appeared.

“I’ve seen it over greasepaint,” continued Hugh. “I’ve seen it stabbed by a Moor, poisoned by a duke, crowned by a ghost, and chased round a stage by a man dressed as a bear.”

“Treason!” said Ana-Pest, but without confidence.

“You’re Tim Hurlygurly,” cried Hugh, “the playhouse fellow from the Red Cockerel! You played a dead king last winter and sneezed in the coffin. I threw an onion.”

The effect of this disclosure was immediate and remarkable.

The king’s face collapsed beneath his forehead. The queen looked at him; the archduke looked at the queen; Ana-Pest looked at everybody; the Grand Pestifer barked with what sounded suspiciously like laughter. Tem-Pest climbed onto a coffin and began chanting, “Tim! Tim! Tim!” while striking a skull with the marrow-bone.

“Seize the slanderer!” roared the monarch.

“Actor!” shouted Hugh. “Rogue! Cellar-thief! His Majesty of the Warming-Pan!”

“Treason!” screamed the entire court.

The queen, being nearest to Tarpaulin and endowed with an enthusiasm disproportionate even to her bulk, launched herself from her coffins. For one majestic instant she sailed through the ghastly light, veil streaming, bottles rattling, coronet flashing. She struck Hugh amidships. The two revolved together, demolished a trestle, rebounded from the wall, and rolled toward the open ale barrel.

Hugh caught the rim.

The queen sat upon his fingers.

He vanished into the cask with a sound resembling a church organ swallowing a boot.

Legs made no speech. His countenance, ordinarily mournful, assumed that complete vacancy which in certain seamen precedes tempestuous action. He reached across the table, took King Pest by the coffin-handle chain, lifted him bodily, and deposited him headfirst through an open trapdoor leading to the cellar.

The king’s descent was accompanied by three crashes, an oath of theatrical excellence, and the remote shattering of bottles.

The court rose.

The archduke advanced rigidly, using his nose as a ram. Legs stepped aside. His Grace passed between the tall sailor’s knees and entered the passage, where his coffin stuck crosswise between the upright coffins. Ana-Pest rushed forward, bells jangling, and attempted to bite Legs in the thigh; but his thigh was at a height inconvenient to her, and she secured only a portion of his coat. The Grand Pestifer crawled beneath the table and attacked Legs’s ankles with the thigh-bone sceptre. Tem-Pest climbed the suspended skeleton and shrieked encouragement from its ribs.

Queen Pest-Iferous, having disposed of Hugh, returned with her veil wrapped around one eye and a carving knife in either hand.

Legs looked upward.

The skeleton looked downward.

“Lend us a hand, mate,” said the sailor.

With one pull he tore the skeleton from its hook.

There are weapons whose use is dignified by antiquity—the sword, the pike, the bow, the battle-axe. There are others whose novelty supplies whatever grandeur tradition has denied them. Legs’s employment of a complete human skeleton partook of both descriptions. Grasping it by the spinal column, he swept it around his head with a whistling of bones. The feet struck Ana-Pest and sent her jingling into a stack of child coffins. One arm detached itself, crossed the room, and extinguished a candle. The skull collided with the Grand Pestifer’s mitre, driving the old man backward into the punch bowl. A second revolution removed the queen’s knives and a quantity of her veil.

Tem-Pest, deprived of its perch, clung to the skeleton’s pelvis and described wide circles through the air, crying, “Majesty! Majesty!” at every turn.

The room became a theatre of comprehensive disorder.

The archduke, still wedged in the passage, kicked his legs with great energy and caused the upright coffins to fall one after another, each knocking down its neighbour, until the entire corridor collapsed with a solemn succession of booms. Ana-Pest emerged from the little coffins wearing three of them upon her arms and head. The Grand Pestifer lifted his face from the punch, barked bubbles, and disappeared again. Queen Pest-Iferous seized the funeral pall and cast it over Legs, who for several seconds continued to swing the skeleton beneath a black canopy, looking less like a combatant than an unusually violent tent.

From the barrel came a muffled pounding.

“Hugh!” cried Legs.

The pounding became furious.

He threw aside the pall, released the skeleton, and sprang toward the cask. The queen seized his coat-tails. Ana-Pest seized the queen. Tem-Pest seized Ana-Pest’s winding-sheet. The Grand Pestifer, rising blind and dripping, seized Tem-Pest. Thus connected in a chain of nobility, they were dragged across the floor behind Legs until he reached the barrel.

The cask was immensely heavy. Legs bent his knees, braced his back, and pulled.

Nothing happened.

The queen bit him.

He pulled again.

The barrel tilted an inch.

A deep and aqueous voice from within said, “Heave!”

Legs heaved.

The barrel rose upon its rim, balanced there with deliberation, and overturned.

No ordinary account can adequately represent the consequences. The brown ale came forth not as a beverage but as a liberation. It struck the table, lifted the coffin lids from their trestles, swept bottles, skulls, onions, dice, meat, candles, and royal paraphernalia into one advancing wave, and spread to every quarter of the room. Hugh emerged in the van, seated upright, purple-faced, and blowing foam from his nostrils like a marine deity of low reputation.

The queen, still attached to Legs’s coat, received the first force of the inundation and was floated backward upon a coffin lid. Ana-Pest climbed upon her and rang violently. Tem-Pest rode past in the punch bowl. The Grand Pestifer disappeared beneath a wreath inscribed “Our Loss Is Heaven’s Gain.” The archduke, freed at last from the passage by the pressure of the liquid, shot forward in his coffin garment with the velocity of a launched boat and struck the opposite wall nose first.

Meanwhile the flood poured through the open trapdoor.

From below arose the voice of King Pest.

“Help! Assistance! The monarchy is drowning!”

A succession of empty casks, disturbed by the cataract, rolled in the cellar. The king cried out once, twice, and then emerged through the trapdoor borne upon a rising fermentation of ale, wine, broken bottles, and deceased rats. His warming-pan crown was gone; his petticoat mantle covered his head; and his thigh-bone sceptre, floating beside him, struck him repeatedly upon the forehead as if performing a constitutional rebuke.

“Treason!” he spluttered.

“Treason!” answered the court from various points of wreckage.

“Treason!” echoed Hugh, who had found the word attractive.

The remaining candles hissed out. Only the flame in the skeleton’s skull continued to burn, the skull having lodged upon a shelf above the flood. Its illumination now discovered a scene which, for grandeur of catastrophe and meanness of materials, has perhaps never been surpassed.

The table had collapsed. Coffins sailed in squadrons. The queen revolved slowly upon her lid, using a carving knife as an oar. Ana-Pest clung to the queen’s coronet by her teeth. The archduke lay upon his back, his coffin full of ale, his great nose projecting above the surface like a promontory at high tide. The Grand Pestifer barked from inside a cupboard. Tem-Pest, entirely delighted, navigated the punch bowl around the room by paddling with two dead men’s nameplates. King Pest attempted to mount the trestles, but each time he rose, Legs pushed him down with the skeleton’s detached arm.

Hugh climbed to his feet.

His clothes streamed. His cheeks had lost none of their colour. He opened his mouth, exhaled a quantity of ale, and said:

“Wasteful.”

“Can you walk?” asked Legs.

“Can I walk? I’ve taken a gallon outside and half a barrel inside. I’m ballasted to the eyebrows.”

The queen’s coffin lid collided with him. She caught him by the neck.

“Assassin!” she cried.

Hugh contemplated her single visible eye, her horses’ teeth, her dripping necklace, and the amplitude with which Providence had equipped her.

“Widow?” he inquired.

“Queen!”

“Near enough.”

He put one arm around her waist—or around that portion of it which could be located—and dragged her toward the passage.

Legs, not to be outdone in gallantry, lifted Ana-Pest from the wreckage. The princess shrieked, jingled, kicked him in the ribs, and called upon plague, heaven, hell, and the city constables.

“Quiet,” said Legs. “You’re rescued.”

“From what?”

He looked around the room.

“From society.”

King Pest perceived their intention and rose waist-deep in the flood.

“Villains! Pirates! You dare abduct the sacred women of our house?”

Hugh adjusted the queen beneath his arm as a porter adjusts a parcel.

“Salvage,” said he. “Law of the sea.”

“This is not the sea!”

Hugh pointed to the floating coffins.

“It’s improving.”

The sailors made for the door. The passage was blocked by fallen merchandise, but Legs, using his princess as a counterweight, kicked a path through it. Hugh followed with the queen, who alternately demanded release and instructed him to mind her bottles. Behind them the court attempted pursuit. The archduke could not bend. The Grand Pestifer could not see. Tem-Pest refused to leave the punch bowl. King Pest mounted a coffin, proclaimed himself admiral, and immediately capsized.

Our heroes emerged into Bell-and-Bone Lane.

The night air, foul as it was, seemed wholesome after the vapours of the royal chamber. Dawn had begun to dilute the eastern darkness with a pale green light. Somewhere beyond the barricades a cart bell rang. Somewhere nearer, a window opened and a voice prayed to be taken. The sailors paused only long enough to determine the direction of the river.

“This way,” said Legs.

“That’s north.”

“It feels wet.”

“Everything feels wet.”

They set off, Legs striding with Ana-Pest over one shoulder, Hugh rolling forward beneath Queen Pest-Iferous like a beetle transporting a duchess. Behind them the undertaker’s shop continued to emit cries, splashes, proclamations, barks, and the recurrent chorus of “Treason!”

The plague streets offered no opposition. Death, who had guarded them efficiently against sober men, had made no provision for drunken sailors carrying counterfeit royalty. They passed the coughing bundle, now silent; the corpse beside the pump; the handcart with its covered passengers. Queen Pest-Iferous, sobered by motion, began to give directions.

“Left at the saint without a head,” she said. “Then right by the burned apothecary. There is a breach near the old bakehouse.”

“You know the channel,” said Hugh.

“I have used it before.”

“To enter?”

“To bring in wine.”

“Public service?”

“Of the loftiest description.”

Ana-Pest, dangling down Legs’s back, ceased struggling.

“Where are you taking us?” she demanded.

“To the *Saucy Wench*.”

“What is that?”

“A brig.”

“Is there drink?”

“Rum.”

“Then walk faster.”

They found the breach as the queen had promised—a gap between a cartwheel and two beams. Legs passed through with little difficulty, though Ana-Pest’s ears caught momentarily on either side. Hugh’s passage presented a more serious geometrical problem. He pushed; the queen complained; the barricade creaked. At last a rotten bureau gave way, and sailor, sovereign, woodwork, and several stones rolled together into the healthy portion of London.

A watchman standing nearby raised his lantern.

“Who goes there?”

Legs rose to his full altitude. The lantern illuminated his gaunt, dripping figure, the princess’s enormous ears, Hugh’s purple face, and the queen’s white immensity crowned with horses’ teeth.

The watchman dropped the lantern and fled.

“Proper respect,” said Hugh.

The four continued toward the river through streets just beginning to stir. Bakers’ boys, apprentices, scavengers, early market women, and two minor clerics witnessed their passage. Each received a different explanation. To one they were ambassadors. To another, shipwrecked nobility. To a third, a wedding party from Limehouse. Hugh told a fishwife that the queen was an imported mermaid; Legs informed a constable that Ana-Pest was a navigational instrument. The constable, observing her ears, admitted that she might be.

At the wharf the tide was turning.

The *Saucy Wench* lay in the grey water, her spars and rigging black against the whitening sky. A sleepy mate leaned over the rail. When he saw Legs and Hugh approaching with their acquisitions, he removed his cap, scratched his head, and shouted:

“What cargo’s that?”

“Royal freight!” called Hugh.

“Dutiable?”

“Not if we stow it quick.”

A boat was lowered. The queen entered it with considerable dignity and displacement; Ana-Pest followed willingly upon learning that the rum was aboard. Legs took the oars. Hugh sat in the stern, still holding the flattened pudding, which by some miracle of devotion had remained in his possession throughout the battle.

As they pulled away, the bells of London began their morning tolling. The sound rolled over roofs and chimneys, over barricades and burial pits, over the undertaker’s ruined shop where King Pest and his family still disputed the succession amid floating coffins. It was a solemn sound, and the river mist received it mournfully.

Hugh listened.

“Funeral?” he asked.

“Likely.”

“Whose?”

Legs considered the great city, pallid beneath dawn, and dipped his oars.

“Everybody’s, sooner or later.”

Hugh accepted this philosophy with a nod, opened the rescued pudding, and offered a portion to the queen.

Thus did Legs and Hugh Tarpaulin escape the dominions of Pest—owing their preservation not to prudence, valour, piety, medical wisdom, or the protection of lawful authority, but to unpaid ale, defective barricades, an actor’s forehead, and the circumstance that a skeleton, though ill-fitted for conversation, may prove an admirable weapon when grasped by the spine.

### The Keeper of Lost Hours

Every morning at six, before the baker lit his ovens and before the ferries began crossing the gray river, Elias Vale climbed the hill to the clock tower and unlocked the door.

The tower had not told the correct time in seventeen years.

Its eastern face was twelve minutes slow, its western face seven minutes fast, and the northern face had stopped entirely at twenty-three minutes past four. The southern clock possessed no hands at all. They had fallen during a storm and buried themselves like spears in the roof of the courthouse below.

Still, Elias wound the mechanism each morning.

He was a narrow man with silver hair and careful hands. In summer he wore a waistcoat the color of dry moss; in winter, a long black coat that made him resemble a shadow returning home. The people of Bellweather knew him as the tower keeper, though few understood what he kept there.

They assumed it was the clock.

It was not.

Behind the clockwork, concealed by a door with no handle, lay a room filled with lost hours.

They stood in bottles along shelves reaching from floor to ceiling. Some glowed gold, some blue, some with the soft red of banked coals. Each bottle bore a paper label written in Elias’s precise hand.

ONE HOUR LOST WAITING FOR A LETTER THAT NEVER CAME.

FORTY MINUTES MISPLACED IN A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR.

A SUMMER AFTERNOON FORGOTTEN BY TWO SISTERS AFTER THEIR QUARREL.

SEVEN MINUTES TAKEN BY FEAR AT THE EDGE OF A DIVING BOARD.

The bottles whispered when Elias passed. If he placed his ear near the glass, he could hear rain on windows, spoons against teacups, the dry cough of an old man, the laugh of a child who had not yet learned to be ashamed of laughing too loudly.

Lost time gathered everywhere, but Bellweather gathered more than most places.

The town stood in a bend of the river where fog lingered even under sunlight. Travelers often missed trains there. Lovers arrived too late. Children spent whole days searching for paths that had never existed. People forgot why they had entered rooms and emerged years older, carrying objects they did not remember picking up.

For three generations, the Vale family had collected these hours. Elias’s grandfather had found them shimmering in gutters and trapped them in jam jars. His father had designed the labels and built the hidden room. Elias had perfected the craft.

A lost minute felt like cool silk between the fingers. An hour had weight. A year could break a man’s back.

There was only one rule: lost time could be returned, but never to the person who had lost it.

“Time remembers the shape of its first owner,” Elias’s father had warned him. “Pour it back into the same life, and it will tear that life open trying to fit.”

So Elias redistributed the hours when they were needed.

He gave a dying mother ten minutes to hear her son’s voice after his ship reached port. He gave a surgeon thirty seconds to catch a mistake. He gave a schoolboy an extra afternoon in which to find his little brother in the woods.

No one knew.

People called such things miracles, luck, or errors in the clocks.

Elias called them bookkeeping.

Then, one November morning, he found a girl sitting on the tower steps.

She was perhaps fourteen, though her solemn expression made her seem older. She wore a red scarf and a blue coat with one missing button. Her dark hair had been cut unevenly, as if she had done it herself without a mirror.

“You’re blocking the door,” Elias said.

“I know.”

“May I ask why?”

“You may.”

She did not move.

Elias waited. The girl looked down at the sleeping town, where chimneys had begun to breathe thin columns of smoke.

“My name is Mara Finch,” she said at last. “You have something that belongs to me.”

Elias felt the tower key grow cold in his hand.

“I repair clocks.”

“No, you don’t. Everyone knows the clocks are wrong.”

“Then you have no reason to trouble me.”

“My mother died yesterday.”

Elias lowered his eyes. Death was common knowledge in Bellweather; grief traveled faster than fire. He remembered hearing that Lenora Finch, the seamstress on Candle Street, had passed after a long illness.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“She lost an hour last Tuesday.”

“Many people lose hours.”

“She was sitting beside the window. I was reading to her. Then the room changed.”

Elias looked at the girl more carefully.

“How?”

“The light jumped. The candle burned lower. The tea went cold. Mother said she could hear bells under the floor.” Mara stood. “Then you walked past our house carrying a black case.”

Elias said nothing.

“I want the hour back.”

“I don’t have it.”

“You’re lying.”

“You should go home.”

“I don’t have a home now. My aunt is selling the house.”

A gust climbed the hill and worried at the end of her scarf. From somewhere near the river came the lonely call of a ferry horn.

Mara held out her hand.

“Give it to me.”

“I can’t.”

“Then give it to someone else and take me to them.”

“It doesn’t work that way.”

“How does it work?”

“It doesn’t.”

She stared at him, furious and wounded. Elias had seen that expression before, on the faces of people who believed the world had made a clerical mistake and could be persuaded to correct it.

He stepped around her and fitted the key into the lock.

Behind him, Mara said, “She was trying to tell me who my father was.”

Elias stopped.

“She’d never told me. That morning she said she would. Then the hour disappeared, and afterward she couldn’t speak.”

The wind moved between them.

“I need to know what she said,” Mara whispered.

Elias entered the tower and closed the door.

For the next six mornings, Mara waited on the steps.

Sometimes she spoke. Sometimes she did not. On the second morning she brought a hammer and threatened to break the door. On the third she brought bread. On the fourth it rained, but she remained until her blue coat was nearly black with water.

On the fifth morning, Elias asked, “Don’t you attend school?”

“Not anymore.”

“Why?”

“I lost patience with it. Do you keep that in a bottle too?”

On the sixth morning, she followed him inside before he could stop her.

The tower’s interior was a hollow cylinder threaded by a spiral staircase. Above them, gears turned with the groaning patience of old animals. Dust trembled from the beams each time the mechanism advanced.

Mara looked upward.

“If the clocks are wrong, why wind them?”

“If I stop, they’ll become more wrong.”

“That’s a poor answer.”

“It’s the only one I have.”

Elias climbed. Mara climbed behind him.

At the first landing, he turned.

“You cannot come farther.”

“Why?”

“Because I said so.”

“My aunt says that when she has no reason.”

“Your aunt sounds wise.”

“She isn’t.”

Elias continued. So did Mara.

At the top of the stairs stood the handleless door. It opened only when Elias pressed his palm to the center and surrendered a minute of his own life. The tower took the minute cleanly. His heart skipped a beat; the light shivered; and the door swung inward.

Mara slipped through beside him.

She stopped breathing.

The room was larger than the tower should have allowed. Shelves vanished into blue distance, crowded with bottles that flickered and murmured. Ladders moved along brass rails without being touched. Paper labels rustled though there was no wind.

At the center stood a long wooden table. On it rested Elias’s black collection case.

Mara took one step forward.

“So I was right.”

“You were persistent.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“Often it is.”

She approached the nearest shelf. A thumb-sized vial glowed with pale green light.

“Can I touch one?”

“No.”

She touched it.

The bottle rang like a tiny bell. Mara jerked back, and for an instant the room smelled of summer grass.

“What was that?”

“A minute lost by a woman named Clara Holt when she saw her future husband for the first time.”

“How do you lose a minute seeing someone?”

“There are many ways.”

Mara moved down the shelf, reading labels.

“Three hours lost in a snowstorm. A morning forgotten after a fever. Twelve minutes stolen by a nightmare.” She looked at him. “Stolen?”

“Time is not always lost by accident.”

“Who steals it?”

“Cruel people. Lonely places. Certain dreams.”

“Clock keepers?”

Elias removed his coat.

“Sometimes.”

She began searching the shelves.

“Your mother’s hour is not here.”

“You said you didn’t have it.”

“I don’t.”

“You collected it.”

“Yes.”

“Then where is it?”

Elias opened the black case. Inside lay empty bottles, silver tongs, labels, sealing wax, and a small compass whose needle pointed not north but toward the nearest fracture in time.

“I used it.”

Mara’s face went still.

“For what?”

“Two nights ago, a ferry rope snapped. A deckhand was pulled into the river. I gave him an hour to reach the bank before the cold stopped his heart.”

“You gave my hour to a stranger?”

“It was not your hour.”

“It was my mother’s.”

“She no longer needed it.”

“I needed it!”

Her shout struck the bottles. Thousands of lost moments whispered awake. The room filled with fragments: a baby crying, a glass breaking, applause in a distant theater, a woman saying wait, please wait.

Mara seized a golden bottle from the shelf.

Elias moved faster than she expected. He caught her wrist.

“Put it down.”

“Give me an hour.”

“No.”

“Any hour.”

“It won’t contain your mother’s words.”

“Maybe I don’t care anymore.”

“You care very much.”

She twisted free. The bottle slipped.

Elias caught it inches above the floor.

The light inside flared. For one heartbeat, they both stood in a kitchen twenty years earlier while a young man peeled apples and sang badly. Then the vision vanished.

Mara was crying.

“I only want to hear her again.”

Elias placed the bottle safely on the table.

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

He looked toward the highest shelves, where the oldest hours glowed faintly behind layers of dust.

“My wife died thirty-one years ago,” he said. “Her name was Iris.”

Mara wiped her face with her sleeve.

“Did she lose any time?”

“Eleven minutes on the day we met. Two days during the birth of our son. Five hours in the summer before she died.”

“Did you keep them?”

“Yes.”

“Did you use them?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I was a coward.”

He took a ladder and pushed it along the rail. It rolled by itself into the blue depths of the room. Elias followed, and after a moment Mara joined him.

They passed years shelved in green demijohns, seconds held in glass beads, and one dark bottle bound in chains. At last Elias stopped before a small locked cabinet.

He opened it.

Inside were three vessels. Two were clear and empty. The third contained a trembling violet light.

“Five hours,” he said.

Mara leaned close.

“What was she doing?”

“Dying.”

The violet light pulsed like a tired heart.

“Iris had a fever. Near the end, she became confused. She thought I was someone else. She begged me to find our son.”

“Where was he?”

“Already dead.”

Mara looked up.

“He had drowned the winter before. He was nine.”

The clockwork groaned beyond the walls.

“I collected those five hours,” Elias continued, “because I could not bear them. I told myself I was preserving her life, but really I was cutting away the part that hurt me.”

“Did it work?”

“No. Pain does not live in time. It lives in us.”

“Then why keep the bottle?”

“Because those were still her hours. Terrible as they were, they belonged to her life. And I loved her whole life, not only the pleasant parts.”

Mara touched the cabinet door but not the bottle.

“Could you give those hours to me?”

“Yes.”

“Would I see her?”

“You would see Iris. You would hear what she heard. You might feel her fever and her fear. Time carries everything.”

Mara stepped back.

“I don’t want that.”

“No.”

They returned to the table. Outside, the clocks began striking seven, though each face started at a different moment. The mismatched bells tumbled over Bellweather.

Mara sat on the floor.

“If my mother’s hour is gone, then her words are gone too.”

“Perhaps.”

“You don’t sound sure.”

“Words are rarely contained in a single hour. People spend years preparing to say important things. They reveal them in pieces without knowing.”

“She never revealed anything about my father.”

“Did she keep letters?”

“My aunt burned them yesterday.”

“Photographs?”

“None.”

“Friends?”

“She stopped seeing them when she became ill.”

Elias considered this.

“What did your mother sew?”

“Clothes.”

“For whom?”

“Everyone.”

“Recently?”

Mara frowned. “She was making a green dress before she became too weak. She worked on it for months, but no one ever collected it.”

“Then perhaps she was not making it for a customer.”

They descended the tower together.

By then Bellweather was awake. Carts rattled over wet stones, shutters opened, and the first ferry drew a white line across the river.

Lenora Finch’s house stood on Candle Street between a cobbler’s shop and a narrow alley. A card in the window announced an estate sale. Mara’s aunt, a severe woman named Agnes, opened the door.

“You again,” she said to Mara.

“I live here.”

“Not after Friday.”

Agnes looked suspiciously at Elias.

“The clocks are worse than ever.”

“I’ll make a note of it,” he said.

Mara pushed inside.

The workroom was almost empty. Bolts of cloth had been sold, drawers emptied, and Lenora’s sewing machine stood under a dust sheet. Only scraps remained on the floor like fallen leaves.

“The green dress,” Elias said.

Agnes crossed her arms. “Useless thing. Odd measurements. No customer wanted it.”

“Where is it?”

“In the rubbish.”

They found the dress in a basket behind the house.

It was beautifully made. Green wool, narrow sleeves, pearl buttons. Far too large for Mara and too small for Agnes. Elias held it up.

“Try it on,” he said.

“It won’t fit.”

“Try.”

Mara changed behind a hanging sheet. As she had predicted, the dress hung loose at the shoulders and reached nearly to her ankles.

“It’s not for me.”

Elias examined the seams.

Lenora Finch had been known for invisible stitching. Yet the hem was clumsy, thick in one place, as if finished by an impatient apprentice.

“Scissors,” he said.

Agnes protested. Mara handed him a pair.

He cut three stitches.

A folded strip of fabric slid from the hem.

On it, in faded ink, someone had written a name.

THOMAS ARDEN, CLOCKMAKER’S APPRENTICE, NORTH QUAY.

Mara read it twice.

“Is that my father?”

“I don’t know,” Elias said.

Agnes sat down heavily on an upturned crate.

“I told her to forget him.”

Mara spun around.

“You knew?”

“He left before you were born.”

“You burned the letters.”

“They were old and private.”

“They were mine!”

“No,” Agnes said, and for the first time her severity cracked. “They were hers.”

Mara clutched the strip of cloth.

“Where is North Quay?”

“Across the river,” Elias said. “Or it was. The district flooded twelve years ago.”

Agnes stared at the green dress.

“Thomas Arden didn’t leave your mother,” she said quietly. “Not in the way she thought. He went to work one morning and never came back.”

“What happened?”

“No one knew. Lenora waited. Then she stopped waiting.”

Mara looked at Elias.

“A lost hour?”

“Perhaps.”

The compass in his black case began to spin.

Elias felt it before he saw it: a looseness in the air, a tremor behind the ordinary ticking of the world. He took out the compass. Its needle pointed toward the river.

They hurried to the quay.

Fog covered the water. Ferries moved as dim shapes between bells. The compass led Elias and Mara past the ticket house, along the embankment, and down a stairway slick with moss.

At the bottom, the river lapped against a bricked-up arch.

“I don’t understand,” Mara said.

Elias pressed his hand to the wall.

It was warm.

“Some lost places continue existing,” he said. “They wait for the missing time to find them.”

“Can we get through?”

“Possibly.”

“How?”

Elias opened his case. He had three empty bottles and no loose hours. Nothing strong enough to open a fracture sealed for more than a decade.

Except the five hours belonging to Iris.

Mara saw his expression.

“No,” she said.

“He may be behind this wall.”

“You said you kept those hours because you loved her whole life.”

“I do.”

“Then don’t use them.”

Elias looked at the bricked arch. From the other side came a faint metallic tapping.

Not random tapping.

A clockmaker’s rhythm.

“I have guarded those hours for thirty-one years,” he said. “I told myself that was love. Perhaps love is not guarding what the dead left behind. Perhaps it is spending it wisely.”

They returned to the tower.

The violet bottle seemed colder when Elias lifted it from the cabinet. For three decades he had imagined opening it. He had feared Iris’s fever, her grief, and the chance that her last hours contained no love for him at all.

Now he carried it to the river.

He broke the seal against the wall.

Violet light poured over the bricks.

For an instant Elias heard Iris calling their son’s name. He smelled medicine and winter roses. He felt her hand gripping his with astonishing strength.

Then the light entered the arch.

The bricks aged in seconds. Mortar crumbled. Moss spread and withered. The river withdrew from a doorway that had not existed a moment before.

Beyond lay a narrow street under a bright summer sky.

Mara took Elias’s hand.

Together they crossed.

North Quay had been preserved inside a missing afternoon. Sunlight shone on shop windows. A dog slept beneath a cart. People stood motionless in the streets, their faces peaceful, as if pausing between one second and the next.

From a workshop came the sound of tapping.

Inside, a man sat at a bench surrounded by clocks.

He was about thirty years old, with dark hair and ink on his sleeves. One hand held a tiny hammer. The other rested beside an unfinished watch.

When Mara entered, he looked up.

“You’re not Master Bell,” he said.

His eyes were the same gray as hers.

Mara could not speak.

Thomas Arden glanced toward the window. “Is something wrong? The light changed.”

Elias stepped forward.

“What date do you think it is?”

Thomas answered.

It was a date fifteen years earlier.

The lost afternoon had closed around North Quay just before the flood. To those trapped within it, less than a minute had passed.

Elias explained slowly.

Thomas did not believe him until Mara showed him the cloth from the green dress.

He recognized Lenora’s handwriting.

“She was going to tell me something,” he said. “She asked me to come after work.”

Mara’s face tightened.

“She died three days ago.”

For Thomas, the words crossed fifteen years in an instant.

He sat down.

The clocks around him ticked, though none of their hands moved.

“I loved her,” he said.

“I know,” Mara replied, though she had not known until then.

The preserved afternoon was collapsing. Buildings flickered. Beyond the windows, summer alternated with floodwater and fog.

“We have to go,” Elias said.

Thomas snatched the unfinished watch from his bench. They ran through the doorway as North Quay began to dissolve. The frozen people vanished into light—not dying, Elias thought, but finally reaching whatever hour had waited for them.

They crossed the arch just before the river broke through.

Cold water knocked Elias to his knees. Mara and Thomas dragged him up the stairs while the bricks sealed behind them. When they reached the embankment, the fog had lifted.

The town clocks were striking noon.

For once, all four faces agreed.

Thomas stood in the pale sunlight, soaked and shivering, a young man in clothes fifteen years out of fashion. Mara faced him with her mother’s name still trembling between them.

Neither knew what to do.

At last Thomas opened his hand.

The unfinished watch lay in his palm.

“I made this for Lenora,” he said. “I meant to finish it that evening.”

Mara touched the cracked glass.

“Can it be repaired?”

Thomas looked toward the clock tower on the hill.

“Yes,” he said. “I think so.”

Years later, people in Bellweather would tell the story differently.

Some said Mara Finch found her father living among river ghosts. Some said Elias Vale stopped a flood by pouring moonlight into the water. Agnes insisted there had never been magic at all, only municipal negligence.

The tower clocks remained unreliable.

The eastern face lost three minutes every winter. The western face gained an hour during thunderstorms. The northern clock resumed at last but refused to acknowledge Tuesdays. New hands were fitted to the southern face, though they sometimes turned backward when anyone in the courthouse told a lie.

Elias retired when he was seventy-nine.

Mara became the next keeper.

Each morning she climbed the hill in a green coat remade from her mother’s dress. She wound the mechanism, dusted the bottles, and listened for lost time gathering in the streets below.

Thomas worked in the room beneath the bells, repairing watches and learning how much the world had changed. He grew older. Mara did too. Neither tried to recover the years between them.

Some absences could not be filled.

Some hours should not be returned.

But on the highest shelf of the hidden room stood a new bottle, glowing violet and gold. Its label, written in Mara’s hand, read:

ONE MINUTE FOUND BETWEEN A FATHER AND DAUGHTER, WHEN BOTH BELIEVED IT WAS TOO LATE.

She never spent it.

She never sealed it away, either.

She kept it near the window, where every morning the light passed through the glass and scattered across the tower walls, turning all the wrong clocks bright.
